bridge: From P03, recognise a list of strings, a function call and None. From P04, run a saved file using built-in modules. Readiness check: if the required length is at least 3, lengths 2, 3 and 4 should be rejected, accepted and accepted. That small decision is a test specification.
teaching:
Begin with a rule a person can check: our identifiers must start with a lowercase letter, contain only lowercase letters or digits, and have 3–8 characters. Before writing code, decide that abc should pass, ab should fail and abc! should fail. A test compares such an expected answer with the function’s observed answer. A failure is useful information about a disagreement, not evidence that you are bad at programming.

A test makes a claim about observable behaviour. Good cases distinguish a correct implementation from realistic mistakes. For a boundary n>=3, test 2,3 and 4 rather than only 100. A test can pass while missing a defect if the chosen inputs never reach the relevant branch.

When debugging, first reproduce the failure with the smallest useful input. Compare expected and observed values, then trace the first point where they diverge. A debugger lets you pause and inspect state; a print can also help if it answers a specific question. Add a regression assertion after the fix so the same behaviour remains checked.

Regular expressions describe text patterns, not arbitrary structured formats. fullmatch requires the whole string to match, while search can find a matching substring. In a simple identifier pattern, brackets form a set of allowed characters, + repeats one or more times and a quantifier applies to the immediately preceding pattern. Length and character policy should be intentional.

The video uses pytest, while this exercise uses Python’s built-in unittest. No pytest installation is required for the supplied exercise. class IdTests(unittest.TestCase) groups tests and obtains assertion helpers from unittest.TestCase. Each def test_... method is one test; self refers to the test instance supplied by the runner. self.assertTrue(value, message) fails if value is false; assertFalse does the reverse. unittest.main() discovers and runs these methods when the file is run directly. This is framework scaffolding; general object-oriented design is studied later.

For standalone assertions, Python can omit assert checks in optimised execution, so never use them as the only input-validation or authorisation check. Test expected failure explicitly and let the test runner report unexpected exceptions. A passing test for one case does not cover another branch; keep expected answers independent from the implementation under test.

Read the regex lecture as a sequence of small experiments, not as a production email validator. r"\." is a raw Python string containing the regex escape for a literal dot; an unescaped dot normally matches any character except newline. In a Python str pattern, \w and \d include Unicode word characters and decimal digits. They are not identical to the ASCII-only [A-Za-z0-9_] and [0-9] unless the matching policy uses re.ASCII. This lesson deliberately uses explicit ASCII ranges.

^ and $ are useful anchors, but $ can match before a final newline; MULTILINE changes their behaviour at line boundaries. fullmatch is the clearer contract for validating the entire identifier. IGNORECASE changes matching, not the stored input; DOTALL changes what dot matches. Select flags deliberately. Do not lower-case an entire email address as a universal identity policy.

search returns a Match object when it finds a match and None otherwise. Parentheses capture a substring: match.group(0) is the whole match, group(1) is the first captured group, and group(2) the next. For example, m = re.fullmatch(r"([A-Z]+):([0-9]+)", "PORT:443") gives m.group(1) == "PORT" and m.group(2) == "443". Check m is not None before reading its groups. A successful substitution does not prove the original input was valid; validate the intended format separately. Regex dialects and engine costs differ. For a URL, email address or structured document, prefer an appropriate parser and explicit policy instead of growing a single regex indefinitely.

Build this pattern one piece at a time. [a-z] accepts one lowercase ASCII letter. [a-z0-9] accepts one lowercase letter or digit. {2,7} repeats only that second piece two through seven times, giving a total length of three through eight. fullmatch tries to match the whole input; “is not None” turns “a match was found” into True. First trace one input by hand, then use the supplied framework to repeat the same checks. You need not design classes yet: keep the IdTests scaffolding and change only the named test cases.
explanation: The first character must be a lowercase letter. It is followed by two through seven lowercase letters or digits, making total length three through eight. abc! is rejected because fullmatch does not ignore the trailing exclamation mark. A search-based implementation would accept a matching substring and violate the contract.
exercise: Save the example as ids_test.py and run it as a module in IDLE, or with the Python command for your environment. It should report OK. In this disposable copy only, replace fullmatch with search and run again: which expected rejection now passes the validator? Restore fullmatch. Add "ABC", "a b", "" and "abc\n" to the list that should be rejected; the last contains a newline escape. Predict all four results first. Check that each test’s expected answer comes from the stated identifier rule, not from copying the function’s current result.
solution: abc! exposes the search mistake. ABC, a b and the empty string are rejected under this policy. Restoring fullmatch makes all expected cases pass. A valid identifier is not by itself proof of authorisation.
challenge: Define valid_port(text) accepting only decimal text whose numeric value is 1 through 65535, with no spaces or sign. Supply tests for "0","1","65535","65536","-1"," 80" and "x".
challenge_solution: Accept "1" and "65535"; reject the others. Validate the text syntax first, then convert and check range. Explain whether non-ASCII decimal characters are allowed by your chosen predicate; an ASCII-only regex [0-9]+ makes the policy explicit. A minimal ASCII policy is: return re.fullmatch(r"[0-9]+", text) is not None and 1 <= int(text) <= 65535. This deliberately accepts leading zeros; state and test a stricter policy if they should be rejected. Add a non-ASCII digit case and a trailing-newline case to distinguish the chosen contract.
